# Supplementary Note 1. Scope, sample identities and source tables

The primary manuscript analyzes seven water samples and a separate set of 77,951 reference phage genomes. The two arms share no sampling frame, no annotation pipeline and no pooled estimate; nothing below combines them into an estimate of a water-treatment effect. The reference collection is restricted to genomes classified as complete, so it occupies the region of recovery that the local catalogue barely reaches. Separate controlled sequence panels, called B and C below, calibrate particular sequence-processing endpoints and do not add environmental samples to either arm. Figure scripts reproduce the displayed summaries from archived tables held inside the project repository. The present integration does not rerun environmental read processing, viral discovery or the original reference-genome model fits. The local model refits and controlled sequence analyses described in Notes 4 and 8 are separately documented calculations.

The `F*_inputs.tsv` and `SF1_community_context_inputs.tsv` files in the same directory contain the plotted values; `F2_community_context_inputs.tsv` keeps its original name and is the input to Supplementary Figure S1, which was Figure 2 before the 2026-09-17 renumbering. The current figure provenance record, with a checksum for every figure input, is generated with the figures at `analyses/data/970-manuscript-figures/figure_provenance.tsv`. Figure files superseded by the 2026-09-17 renumbering, and their input tables, were moved to `analyses/archive/figs-legacy/` and are listed with their checksums in `LEDGER.tsv` there; nothing was deleted.

The written pre-registrations in `outputs/preregistration/` cover the defense census, the Dpd island screen and a gut-depletion comparison. None covers the unit-definition comparison of Note 5 or the completeness analysis of Note 4, which is why the manuscript grades the status of its definitions rather than describing them uniformly as declared in advance. The later B and C1 analysis contracts froze the controlled-panel designs before their respective outcome annotations. The C1 contract also fixed the joint local refit and the retrospective transport of the already observed B results; it did not make those earlier observations prospective.

# Supplementary Note 2. Community context and the dispersion diagnostic

![Community context in the seven-sample survey. Marginal variance shares and nominal p values for location and descriptive water condition under the primary Aitchison distance, together with the alternative viral distance summaries. All comparisons use seven samples. Location and water condition have two and one degrees of freedom respectively, and the displayed variance shares are not a test of relative causal importance.](figures/SF1_community_context.png){#sfig-sf1 width=100%}

Counts were rarefied without replacement to the minimum library depth (63,564 reads for 16S and 53,257 for the full 18S dataset, random seed 20260502) for alpha-diversity and phylogenetic-distance analyses only; relative abundance and centered log-ratio values were calculated independently of rarefaction with a pseudocount of one. The microeukaryotic 18S view excluded records assigned to Metazoa and recalculated both after subsetting, so its rarefied totals need not remain equal across samples.

Only the parametric column of the dispersion output is quoted anywhere in this package, and Table S3 is the archived three-column snapshot (`experiment`, `diss_x_group`, `p_betadisper`) that all quoted values come from. The eight-column specification written into the diversity module, which adds a `permutest` variant and a bias-adjusted variant, had never executed: the chunk referred to a seed argument that existed only as a formal of the enclosing function. That defect was repaired on 2026-09-17 by reading the value the function signature already declared, leaving the permutation count, the dispersion centre and the bias-adjustment setting untouched, and the module now runs. Its parametric column reproduces the archived values digit for digit, which is why no quoted number in this package changes. The permutation and bias-adjusted columns are therefore first-hand as of that date, but no statement here rests on them: for every location contrast the permutation p equals $1.98\times10^{-4}$, which is $1/7!$, the smallest value the exhaustive permutation distribution of seven samples can take, so these results attain the minimum reported permutation p value. That floor limits numerical resolution; it does not by itself invalidate the test or establish an absence of power. The parametric values for the virome are $1.26\times10^{-4}$ for location under Bray-Curtis, $9.17\times10^{-5}$ under Jaccard and $4.00\times10^{-4}$ under Aitchison distance.

Cross-assay concordance under Aitchison distance was strongest between the bacterial and microeukaryotic profiles (Mantel $r=0.699$, nominal $p=0.002$); viral-bacterial concordance was weaker ($r=0.416$, $p=0.115$) and viral-microeukaryotic weaker still ($r=0.129$, $p=0.328$). Procrustes correlations on all six available principal-coordinate dimensions were 0.922, 0.928 and 0.945. These summaries share the same seven samples and are not independent validation assays.

# Supplementary Note 3. Local quality and annotation denominators

The original CheckV counts are 167 complete, 142 high-quality, 450 medium-quality, 2,254 low-quality and 47 undetermined records, summing to 3,060. Low-quality records are 73.7% of the catalogue, so it is not a set of near-complete genomes, and percentage completeness is a separate field: the 75-100% sensitivity bin is not equivalent to the complete or high-quality class. Every population used as a denominator in the manuscript is listed with its meaning and source in Table S16, and each claim with its numerator, denominator and required qualification in Table S17.

The completeness comparison excludes the 47 records without an estimate and contains 3,013 vOTUs. Within the four bins the predicted-temperate carrier and total counts are 6/68, 3/69, 4/51 and 6/72, and the putatively virulent counts 26/1,061, 27/1,056, 15/301 and 26/335. Zero-hit records remain in mean-density denominators (Table S5). Table S23 gives unbinned completeness against per-kilobase hit density; the four bins are a presentation choice, not the analysis. The 19 predicted-temperate carriers in these bins cannot be replaced by the five predicted-temperate carriers from the strict annotation layer: the two counts answer questions under different matching definitions.

The four nominal within-bin Mann-Whitney p values are 0.00197, 0.361, 0.399 and 0.903. The 4,000-resample percentile intervals describe resampling of vOTUs within the observed lifestyle groups, not an uncertainty distribution over independently sampled environments or evolutionary lineages. A lower bound of zero in the second bin is retained because only three predicted-temperate records in that bin carry a match.

*The DRAM-v and VIBRANT annotation denominator.* Table S21 carries six parallel counts. The manuscript quotes the recomputed catalogue-restricted value of 147 vOTUs. The archived value of 146 is kept beside it: both counts use the same recipe and the same vOTU unit, so the discrepancy is not a unit convention, and no recipe in this repository reproduces 146. Its origin is undetermined and is recorded as such rather than explained away. The genuine unit difference in that table is between the unrestricted count of 164 vcontigs and the catalogue-restricted count of 147 vOTUs.

# Supplementary Note 4. Sensitivity of the lifestyle contrast to annotation boundaries and labels

## 4.1 The label depends on completeness

The four-annotator union calls 6.023%, 6.133%, 14.489% and 17.690% of records temperate across the four bins (Table S10, which also gives each annotator's rate). Pooling the two lower bins against the two upper gives 6.078% against 16.206%, a ratio of 2.666. The two protein-content annotators each rise about three-fold on their own, so this is not one tool's artefact but a property of the evidence a fragment can display.

## 4.2 Six definitions, six answers

`S3_label_definitions.tsv` (S7) records the six rules and their genome requirements; `S3_ratios_by_definition.tsv` (S8) gives the ratio, bootstrap interval and Mann-Whitney p for each definition in each bin. In the first completeness bin the ratios are 5.390 for the published union (95% interval 1.142-12.304), 1.296 for Replidec alone, 1.499 for VIBRANT alone, 1.644 for both the two-annotator and the conjunction rules, and 27.215 for integration evidence alone. Only the published union and the integration-evidence definition have any first-bin interval excluding one, and the integration-evidence definition has only ten predicted-temperate records in that bin, four of them carriers. Four of the six definitions therefore provide no first-bin excess that could decay across the completeness gradient.

## 4.3 The 19 CheckV-provirus records, and what the recovered coordinates show

`S3_provirus_confound_audit.tsv` (S11) lists them individually. All 19 are called temperate; estimated contamination runs from 6.34% to 43.94% of contig length; and they are the only records in the catalogue of 3,060 with non-zero estimated contamination. Eight of them carry at least one filtered VFDB-A hit.

The CheckV `region_coords_bp` output, which the integrated database did not retain, was recovered from the original CheckV contamination table and matched to the DRAM-v gene calls that produced each virulence-factor hit. Hits must be located by their own DRAM-v coordinates: the geNomad protein carrying the same index disagrees for 22 of the 143 catalogue hits, and a positional test built on the geNomad indices produces negative margins and cannot be used. Of the 20 hits on provirus contigs, 18 lie wholly inside a predicted host region, one crosses the boundary and one lies wholly inside a predicted viral region. The crossing hit has 581 nt inside the host region and 10 nt inside the viral region; the hit inside the viral region is a second match on the same vOTU and is an unexplained homologous match, not a confirmed virulence gene. The remaining 123 catalogue hits can only be described as not detected inside a predicted host region, which is not the same as confirmed viral origin. Every count in this note is on the 143-hit catalogue frame (20 located plus 123 not detected); the 142-hit analysis frame used by the models is the same set minus one hit, on `vOTU2169`, whose record carries no CheckV completeness estimate and is therefore outside the 3,013 modelled rows.

Refitting an otherwise identical negative-binomial model under six model scenarios, comprising the original analysis and five sensitivity variants, gives the following (Tables S9 and S31; the archived pre-refit model summaries are in Table S6).

| Treatment | n | Additive lifestyle IRR | 95% Wald interval | Nominal p |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Original hits and lengths | 3,013 | 2.520701 | 1.507-4.217 | $4.284\times10^{-4}$ |
| Delete the 19 provirus records | 2,994 | 1.020319 | 0.540-1.928 | 0.951 |
| Remove host-region hits, full length retained | 3,013 | 1.113 | 0.607-2.038 | 0.730 |
| **Keep the predicted viral region on both sides** | **3,013** | **1.049622** | **0.568-1.941** | **0.877** |
| As above but retaining the boundary-crossing hit | 3,013 | 1.139 | 0.622-2.087 | 0.672 |
| Shrink the denominator only | 3,013 | 2.816 | 1.681-4.718 | $8.4\times10^{-5}$ |

Two properties of this ladder matter more than any single row. The trimmed refit retains all 3,013 records, so the result cannot be attributed to losing 0.63% of the sample; its interval is narrower than that obtained by deleting the records, but remains compatible with substantial effects in either direction. Neither interval comparison establishes equivalence or adequate power. Shrinking the denominator of a suspect numerator *enlarges* the effect, so an inflated per-kilobase denominator is not what produces it. In the interaction model, the trimmed fit gives incidence-rate ratios of 1.064, 1.055, 1.046 and 1.036 at 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% completeness, all with intervals spanning one. The strict annotation layer is too sparse to adjudicate anything: 2.320 (0.863-6.236) originally and 1.597 (0.551-4.630) after trimming.

Two adverse robustness variants of this ratio appeared in earlier drafts, quoted as 1.823 ($p=0.037$) and then as 1.686 (0.956-2.974, $p=0.071$). The first added hits back to the numerator without restoring the corresponding length to the denominator. The second has no generator in this repository and is not among the six archived scenarios in `dev/280-publication-stage-a/local/models.tsv`, so it could not be reproduced. Both are withdrawn and no adverse variant is quoted in their place. No claim is made that the trimmed value is significantly below 2.52.

A 200-repetition cluster bootstrap over the existing VC_id assignments gives percentile intervals of 1.389-4.322 for the original fit and 0.481-1.943 for the trimmed fit, with 200 of 200 repetitions converging. With 2,988 clusters over 3,013 records and a maximum cluster size of three, this is not an adequate phylogenetic control. Leaving out one provirus record at a time moves the original IRR only between 2.075 and 2.534, so the effect is not the property of a single record.

## 4.4 The grouping label shares a term with the numerator

The composite temperate label is a disjunction of four conditions, one of which is `checkv_provirus == "Yes"` — an assertion that the record still carries untrimmed bacterial host sequence. The numerator of the contrast is a count of matches to a bacterial virulence-factor library. In the 3,013-record analysis set the four disjuncts fire 201, 2, 19 and 232 times, and fire alone 11, 1, 16 and 40 times. All 19 CheckV-provirus records are labelled temperate, and 16 of them have no other temperate evidence at all: Replidec and VIBRANT both call them lytic and geNomad does not call a provirus.

The 142 filtered VFDB-A hits in the analysis set split as 20 on temperate provirus records, 15 on other temperate records and 107 on virulent records. The temperate arm of 260 records therefore holds 35 hits, of which 20 (57.14%) sit on those 19 records — and those 20 hits come from only eight contigs.

Deleting the provirus disjunct and refitting the identical model (`MASS::glm.nb(N ~ lifestyle + checkv_completeness + offset(log(kb)))`, same 3,013 rows, 16 records relabelled temperate-to-virulent and none in the other direction) gives an incidence-rate ratio of 0.950811, Wald interval 0.4917-1.8386, profile-likelihood interval 0.4827-1.7992, $p=0.8808$. The alternative-label temperate arm has 244 records, 16 hits and 12 carriers.

**This interval is wider than the published one**, 1.3189 against 1.0290 on the log scale, because the temperate arm loses 19 of its 35 hits. This wider interval further limits precision; as with region trimming in Note 4.3, the result establishes sensitivity to the definition, not equivalence between lifestyles. It is not evidence that the effect is absent.

Deleting records, changing the label and trimming to the predicted viral region are complementary sensitivity analyses of the same records and annotation outputs, not independent validation datasets. They are not combined into a single statistic or cited as independently confirming one another.

We additionally crossed the two lifestyle definitions with the two count/length definitions on the same 3,013 records, retaining the original completeness covariate in every model (Table S34). Region correction excludes host-region and boundary-crossing hits and uses the predicted viral length; records without a detected host region retain their original counts and lengths. This rule does not confirm an absence of host sequence on those records. The four model estimates are shown below and in Supplementary Figure S2.

| Lifestyle label | Count and length definition | Predicted-temperate records | Total hits in the model | Lifestyle IRR | 95% Wald interval |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Original four-way union | Original | 260 | 142 | 2.520701 | 1.507–4.217 |
| Original four-way union | Predicted viral region | 260 | 123 | 1.049622 | 0.568–1.941 |
| Union without CheckV provirus term | Original | 244 | 142 | 0.950811 | 0.492–1.839 |
| Union without CheckV provirus term | Predicted viral region | 244 | 123 | 1.003192 | 0.532–1.893 |

All four models converged without warnings. Changing both definitions did not restore the original point estimate of enrichment. These models assess linked definition changes, not independently randomized interventions, and do not separate causal contributions or establish lifestyle equivalence. The 123 hits retained by the corrected model are not the same set as the 123 catalogue hits without a detected host region in Note 4.3; the equal counts must not be used interchangeably. None of these models reruns lifestyle prediction on trimmed sequence.

![Joint sensitivity to lifestyle labels and count/length definitions (Supplementary Figure S2). Points show predicted-temperate versus putatively virulent incidence-rate ratios from four negative-binomial models on the same 3,013 catalogue records; bars are individual 95% Wald intervals. The original completeness covariate is held fixed. The label change removes only the CheckV provirus term from the four-way union; region correction removes host-region and boundary-crossing hits and restricts the length denominator to predicted viral regions where such regions were called. ## 4.5 What the boundary evidence cannot be asked to do

*Circularity.* CheckV partitions a contig by whether each gene resembles bacterial or viral marker sets, and a VFDB-A hit is by construction a match to a bacterial gene. The two are not independent evidence. One provirus contig has a two-gene host region in which both genes are the two VFDB-A hits; another has a three-gene host region with two hits. The correct statement is that the hit positions are consistent with the retained-host-flank reading. No p value from a uniform-placement null model is reported, because such a model assumes exactly the independence that does not hold here.

*Pseudoreplication.* The 20 hits come from eight contigs, in groups of 5, 5, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1 and 1. Virulence-factor genes cluster on bacterial chromosomes, so neighbouring genes in one operon enter and leave together. Treating the 20 hits as independent events can overstate precision. Historical per-hit tests are retained for audit in Table S12 and below, but are not used to support current inference. A whole-contig circular-shift permutation of all hits on a contig, quoted in an earlier draft at $P\approx10^{-5}$, is withdrawn: no script for it exists in this repository or in the code package, and it is not reproduced here. The one contig-level quantity retained is a two-by-two table of the CheckV provirus flag against carriage of at least one filtered VFDB-A hit, 8 of 19 against 105 of 2,994, giving a conditional odds ratio of 19.9 (Fisher $p=1.6\times10^{-7}$). Its estimand is the association between the provirus flag and hit carriage, which is the confounding described above. It is not a test of where hits fall within a contig, and it cannot be used to answer the circularity it illustrates. It is reported here rather than in the main text for that reason.

*The category-composition comparison.* Six of the 20 hits on provirus contigs fall in the VFDB motility category against two of the other 123, again on the 143-hit catalogue frame of Note 4.3. Motility and adhesion functions are typical of bacterial chromosomes, so the direction is consistent with host origin. The comparison is post hoc, rests on eight motility hits distributed over the same eight contigs, and is reported descriptively; it does not establish that these are host genes.

*A second caller and the partition.* Three contigs are called proviruses by both CheckV and VIBRANT. Only one of them, `vctg3638`, has a VIBRANT excision boundary; on that contig the VIBRANT viral interval, nucleotides 1–18,927 of 22,762, lies within the CheckV-predicted viral interval and here shares both of its end coordinates. Agreement between two callers on one contig does not validate the boundary. The comparison is regenerated from the 2 May 2026 VIBRANT 1.2.1 outputs and the recovered CheckV coordinates by `dev/370-audit-integration-2026-09-26/vibrant_checkv_boundary.py`. On the other two, `vctg0998` and `vctg1163`, VIBRANT calls the whole scaffold lysogenic and returns no coordinates, so a segment-level comparison is not defined for them and none is reported. An earlier draft quoted three percentages, 100%, 89.2% and 100%, for this comparison; the middle value has no source in this repository and all three are withdrawn. What survives concerns one contig, and it says nothing about whether any individual virulence-factor hit is a host gene.

*The positional proxy is superseded.* Before the coordinates were recovered, the only available proxy was the relative position of each hit along its contig, which gives a median edge distance of 0.2222 on provirus contigs against 0.2203 elsewhere (Wilcoxon $p=0.7799542$). That test does not discriminate, and it is retained in Table S12 only to record what was available at the time.

**The two sets of 19 are different sets.** Nineteen records are CheckV proviruses with non-zero contamination; nineteen predicted-temperate records carry a filtered VFDB-A match, distributed six, three, four and six across the completeness bins. Their intersection is eight genomes. The coincidence of size is arithmetical and must never be compressed into one clause.

None of the above establishes that every region prediction is correct, that every virulence-factor match is a false positive, or that the true difference between the two lifestyle groups is zero. The lifestyle label is still a full-length composite prediction; lifestyle was not re-predicted on trimmed sequence, and unknown contamination, assembly error and functional ground truth were not measured.

# Supplementary Note 5. Definition-specific reference-genome sensitivity

The reference subset was drawn from MetaVR [@metavr2026]. The primary presentation compares 285 metabolic-related Pfam domains with 38 individual anti-defense-related profiles at the same unit level. The mixed definition applies category pooling before the minimum-carrier criterion, so it is not a controlled pooling experiment restricted to the same 38 profiles. Structural facts about the fitted models, which should be read before interpreting any slope, are listed in Table S27.

| Unit definition | Anti-defense units | Anti-defense median | Metabolic median | Difference | Permutation diagnostic |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Mixed (earlier grouping rule) | 22 | 0.522686 | 4.048350 | 3.525664 | $1/10{,}001$ (Monte Carlo floor) |
| Profile (primary) | 38 | 1.356949 | 4.048350 | 2.691402 | $1/10{,}001$ (Monte Carlo floor) |
| *Withdrawn: named subset* | *25* | *2.788110* | *4.048350* | *1.260240* | *never tested; none exists* |

The reportable interval is therefore 2.691402 to 3.525664, a factor of 1.3100. The permutation entries are the plus-one estimate $(b+1)/(10{,}000+1)$ with $b=0$, whose smallest attainable value is $1/10{,}001$. These finite Monte Carlo estimates attain their numerical floor; they are not confidence bounds on the exact permutation tail probability. Their interpretation additionally requires exchangeability, which is not established for the two libraries, and they do not account for dependence among features measured in the same genomes.

## 5.1 Why the named-profile row is withdrawn

The named definition was obtained by looking each of the 38 profile names up in the anti-defense category table `family_category.tsv` and keeping the 25 that were found. That table is keyed on family and subtype names: of its 666 keys, only 141 are also profile names, and 525 are not, including composite subtypes such as `vcrx089_090`, `vcrx091_093`, `tad2_acriia7`, `arda_ardu` and `Adnd_p0020_p0021`, and the catch-all subtype `Aca_alone`, which is where `aca1`, `aca10`, `aca11` and `aca13` live. Expanding each subtype to its member profiles through the frozen census (`census_systems.tsv`, column `all_profiles`) gives all 38 profiles a category, with none mapping to more than one, and all 195 frozen subtypes resolve to a category. The 25-against-13 split was therefore produced by string matching, not by the annotations, and the difference of 1.260240 it yielded was never covered by a permutation test. The row is kept in Table S25 with `calibre_status = join_artifact` and the join key that produced it, so that the withdrawn wording — "1.26 to 3.53, a 2.8-fold span" — remains auditable. The corrected mapping was cross-checked against a map built independently on another analysis line, which agrees profile by profile over the 166 profiles it covers.

A leave-out sensitivity analysis removing `aca1`, `aca10`, `aca11` and `aca13`, which are accessory markers of anti-CRISPR loci and are treated as separate units only because of the 30-carrier threshold, moves the mixed difference from 3.525664 to 2.964365 and the profile difference from 2.691402 to 2.261736. This is a sensitivity analysis on unit membership, not a third calibre and not a correction to the reported interval, and nothing about the $\ln 10$ benchmark follows from it: $\ln 10$ is a benchmark on the slope axis, not on a difference between two medians.

## 5.2 The benchmark, dispersion and aggregation

Strict proportionality between carriage odds and called gene count corresponds to a slope of $\ln 10\approx2.302585$, not to unity. The metabolic median slope of 4.048350 lies above it and the anti-defense median lies below it under both reportable definitions (1.356948 and 0.522686); these are descriptive medians without intervals, and 26 of the 38 profiles have positive slopes, so the set cannot be described as one in which nothing scales. Class dispersion is not reported as a result: the interquartile-range ratio between the two classes (1.2477) is smaller than the ratio of their median standard errors (1.5726), so the observed difference in spread is within what the difference in estimation precision can produce.

Table S22 (`S9_aggregation_effects.tsv`) gives the nine merged anti-defense categories with their member profiles, member medians and aggregation effects, including categories with a single eligible member and one with none. The reconciliation in that table deliberately retains the archived job's own string-join membership, because its purpose is to reconcile with that job; the corrected census-based membership is carried in parallel columns of the same table. Any statement about the member dispersion of a merged category must say which membership it uses. Two archived jobs return different merged slopes for two categories, differing by 0.011 log-odds for one and by 0.427 for the other, enough to reverse the sign of that category's aggregation effect. Both values are carried with a disagreement flag, neither is preferred, no average is taken, and no merged-category slope is quoted in the manuscript.

## 5.3 Lineage estimability, and why the direction is descriptive only

This is the most fragile point in the reference-genome argument, and it is not fixable by computation. Selecting one genome from each shared-content similarity cluster and repeating 50 times leaves the complete unit set estimable in only 10 repetitions; a 200-repetition bootstrap over 30,079 clusters leaves it estimable in only 76. The carriers of several anti-defense units come from a single cluster: all 73 carriers of `gp4.5`, 42 of `ddra`, 41 of `darb` and 50 of `samase`, with `hdf` at 58 carriers in two clusters, `acrva1` at 33 in three and `ocr` at 62 in four. A repetition that does not sample such a cluster contains no positives for that unit at all, so neither additional iterations nor a different estimator can manufacture independent biological replicates, and the percentile range of the successful subset is not a confidence interval for the full set. The repetition counts are read from the `resampling` block of `dev/280-publication-stage-a/global_primary/summary.json` (mode `representative`, B = 50, 10 valid repetitions; mode `cluster_bootstrap`, B = 200, 76 valid repetitions) and the carrier and cluster counts from `dev/280-publication-stage-a/global_primary/profile_cluster_support.tsv`.

An earlier draft also quoted a simulated probability that the anti-defense median exceeds $\ln 10$, given as 0.456, and a unit-level bootstrap 95% interval for the class difference of 1.243 to 2.951. Neither has a generator in this repository, and neither could be recovered from the archived unit estimates and standard errors under the estimator the draft itself described; both are withdrawn rather than restated, and no replacement value is quoted. A Firth-penalised refit of all 323 features returns valid fits for all of them (969 of 969 across three model forms) and does not reverse the descriptive ordering under adjustment for recorded habitat category or host phylum, with class differences of 2.695592, 2.902745 and 2.524090 at the profile definition. This bounds two coarse covariates. It is not a demonstration of lineage independence, of equal database detectability, or of a causal mechanism.

## 5.4 Sensitivity analyses that belong to the mixed definition

| Recorded ecosystem category | Genomes | Evaluable metabolic domains | Evaluable mixed anti-defense units | Difference between medians |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Aquatic | 29,882 | 238 | 17 | 3.1180 |
| Mammals: Human | 19,768 | 143 | 17 | 3.2521 |
| Terrestrial | 12,323 | 167 | 14 | 2.2813 |
| Plants | 4,511 | 105 | 11 | 1.6588 |
| Mammals | 3,881 | 81 | 7 | 3.2830 |
| Artificial ecosystem | 2,878 | 87 | 9 | 1.1818 |
| Wastewater+WWTP, descriptive subset | 1,036 | 43 | 6 | 2.5662 |

The first six categories satisfy the archived eligibility criteria of at least 2,000 genomes, 20 metabolic domains and five mixed anti-defense units. The wastewater and treatment-plant subset contains 1,036 of 77,951 genomes (1.33%) and meets both annotation criteria — 43 evaluable metabolic domains and six evaluable mixed anti-defense units, with a median difference of 2.5662 in the same direction as every other row — and fails only the 2,000-genome threshold. An earlier draft described it as contributing zero eligible anti-defense units; that reading came from a Boolean eligibility flag of 0 and is corrected here. It remains a descriptive subset of the reference collection rather than a stratum of the local survey, it is not an additional mutually exclusive stratum in a summed total, and no statement about reclaimed water follows from it. Within-stratum evaluability depends on carrier counts, so feature sets vary among rows and the table does not compare absolute prevalence between habitats.

In the archived summary of 50 cluster-representative subsamples, every mixed-unit median difference was positive, with a median of 2.77 and an empirical 2.5th-97.5th percentile range of 2.60-2.92. Each subsample included one genome from each of 30,079 similarity clusters, and evaluable feature counts changed to 260-269 metabolic domains and 18 mixed anti-defense units. The interval is therefore not a confidence interval for a fixed full-set contrast. Exact replication of that historical summary remains unresolved: the currently saved selections produce a slightly different median and percentile range, documented in Note 11. The new domain-composition analysis uses those saved selections and is a separate sensitivity analysis.

**Both of these checks were computed under the mixed unit definition only.** Neither result transfers to the 38-profile primary presentation. Its separate lineage-resampling attempts and limited estimability are described in Note 5.3; the mixed-definition habitat summary does not resolve those limitations.

# Supplementary Note 6. Abundance scale and pseudocount check

Let $x$ be a sample's positive-scale cargo vector and $c$ the sample-specific factor relating the alternative normalization, so that the corresponding vector is $cx$. When zeros are present, applying the same numerical pseudocount to both expressions yields $\operatorname{clr}(x+1)$ and $\operatorname{clr}(cx+1)$, which need not agree, whereas transforming the pseudocount with the same factor yields $\operatorname{clr}(cx+c)=\operatorname{clr}(x+1)$.

The observed per-sample ratios between the two cargo scales were constant to numerical precision (Table S15). Fixed-one CLR maximum absolute discrepancies ranged from 0.266 to 6.537; scaling the pseudocount with the same factor reduced all discrepancies below $2\times10^{-15}$. This identifies the numerical origin of the apparent distinction between the two matrices. It neither establishes a universally optimal zero-replacement method nor reconstructs an absolute environmental concentration.

# Supplementary Note 7. NARP, Dpd and system-call evidence boundaries

NAD-reconstitution pathways have been characterized in published work [@osterman2024]. Under the archived module-calling definition for the 77,951 reference genomes, NARP1 and NARP2 were called in 566 and 166 genomes respectively, with no joint call. These are definition-specific carriage observations. The NARP-focused cross-catalogue comparison did not meet its recorded replication criterion; some estimates were imprecise and one catalogue contained too few NARP2 carriers for an estimate. Neither the absence of a joint call nor a difference in carriage associations establishes a new mechanism in the local water catalogue. Separately, the six NAD-pathway domains all lie above the metabolic median, and removing them moves that median from 4.048350 to 3.982495 (Table S26), so the class difference is not produced by them; equally, this does not certify their category assignment.

The frozen Dpd island-model screen reported 16 model-positive contigs among 24,429,973 assessable contigs, corresponding to 15 vOTUs among 12,705,385 source vOTUs. Ten candidates permitted the relevant contextual assessment and six did not, and none had affirmative evidence placing the candidate in the viral portion of the contig. This is not evidence that all 16 are nonviral, and the large denominator cannot estimate the prevalence of related DNA-modification pathways, because the model covers only a subset of possible architectures.

The associated defense census froze 33 types, 195 subtypes and 356 profiles. Its primary and sensitivity configurations were not consistently separated in the archived aggregation, and the cross-library mapping was not restricted throughout to the frozen model set. Its total system count, agreement fractions and derived type-level comparison are therefore not used as established quantitative findings here. This exclusion concerns configuration provenance, not a claim that every individual model call is false.

# Supplementary Note 8. Controlled sequence calibration, length transport and recovery limits

## 8.1 Two reference panels with known construction origins

The exploratory panel B and the subsequent panel C examine sequence processing under controlled fragmentation and added bacterial flanks. They use known source coordinates to distinguish viral-source from bacterial-chromosome-source bases. This construction information is separate from the predicted region assignments in the environmental catalogue (Note 4). It does not establish natural prophage boundaries, biological function or the correctness of all local host-region predictions. Chromosome-derived fragments can themselves contain mobile elements; construction origin is not a complete evolutionary classification of their genes.

Panel B selected 30 complete RefSeq phage genomes, 30–250 kb long, with unambiguous nucleotides and annotated coding sequences: ten associated with each of the bacterial host genera Escherichia, Pseudomonas and Bacillus. A fixed seed/hash ordering and nucleotide clustering with MMseqs2 [@steinegger2017mmseqs2] (version 18.8cc5c, `easy-cluster`, 95% minimum identity, 85% coverage in target-coverage mode, cluster mode 2) selected distinct clusters without reference to subsequent VFDB results. Each parent supplied contiguous windows containing 25%, 50%, 75%, 90% and 100% of its sequence, with two offsets at each nonfull fraction and one full sequence, yielding 270 viral windows. Adding 0%, 10% or 20% bacterial sequence as a fraction of total construct length produced 810 constructs, with rounding to integer base counts. The three fixed chromosome backgrounds were Escherichia coli K-12 (NC_000913.3), Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1 (NC_002516.2) and Bacillus subtilis 168 (NC_000964.3). They are genus-matched backgrounds, not experimentally established cognate strains. Windows were averaged within parents, with equal weights for the five fragment fractions and the 30 parents; descriptive intervals used 200 parent-genome bootstrap resamples. The 810 constructs are repeated perturbations of 30 parents.

The C1 protocol was frozen before annotating panel C. It used the same source snapshot and eligibility rules, excluding the B accessions, sequences and viral genera, and excluding clusters shared with B under the same 95%/85% thresholds. The resulting 30 additional parents represented 15 viral genera, with five viral genera and ten parents per bacterial host genus. Selection used fixed seeds and source taxonomy, not subsequent VFDB or CheckV outcomes. These viral genera were held out relative to B, not relative to the CheckV database or an independently sampled viral phylogeny.

Panel C used viral windows of 12.5, 17.5, 30, 60 and 120 kb, with two fixed offsets where a parent was long enough. Unavailable lengths were recorded without replacement by other parents. In addition to the original three chromosome backgrounds, the protocol specified E. coli Sakai (NC_002695.2), P. aeruginosa PA14 (NC_008463.1) and B. subtilis 6051-HGW (NC_020507.1). Source sequences were retained unchanged; anchors whose maximum flank would include ambiguous bases were excluded before outcome annotation. Each of the 212 available viral windows was evaluated once without flanks and four times with flanks: 10% and 20% of total length in each of its original and alternative bacterial backgrounds. Thirty full, unflanked parents supplied additional gene-calling baselines, giving $212\times5+30=1,090$ constructs (Table S48). The six fixed chromosomes and their chosen insertion locations do not sample host-strain variation at the population level.

## 8.2 Processing, endpoints and uncertainty

Both panels used CheckV 1.1.1 with database 1.5 [@nayfach2021checkv] and four paired treatments: retain the whole construct; retain the CheckV-predicted viral interval or intervals, keeping the whole construct if no host boundary was found; retain the viral sequence bounded by its known construction coordinates; or discard the whole construct when flagged as a provirus. The third treatment is a known-boundary reference available for constructed sequences, not a deployable method for unknown environmental contigs. Separate retained intervals were processed independently and never concatenated.

Open reading frames (ORFs) were called again with Pyrodigal 3.7.1 in metagenomic mode [@larralde2022pyrodigal] for each distinct retained nucleotide sequence. Sequence-identical outputs could share a recorded computation while preserving the construct/treatment mapping. MMseqs2 searches used the same frozen VFDB Set A protein snapshot, containing 4,755 records [@liu2022vfdb; @steinegger2017mmseqs2]. Filtered matches required at least 30% identity, 70% query coverage and an E-value no greater than $10^{-5}$; the strict layer required at least 40% identity and 80% query coverage at the same E-value threshold. The highest-bit-score passing hit per ORF was retained, breaking ties by E-value and target identifier. Recalled genes were projected back to their source intervals. These matches are homology annotations, not experimentally demonstrated virulence. The new calibration versions and database snapshot do not establish the versions used in the historical environmental annotation pipeline.

Viral-base retention is retained viral-source bases divided by input viral-source bases; host-base removal is removed chromosome-source bases divided by input chromosome-source bases. Host removal is undefined for unflanked inputs. These denominators count sequence, not functions or independent samples. The same nucleotide endpoints appear in both VFDB threshold layers and are used only once in sequence comparisons.

For C, primary analyses used 12.5, 17.5 and 30 kb viral windows. The 36 primary strata cross three bacterial host genera, three window lengths, two flank proportions and two fixed backgrounds; each contains five viral genera, ten parents and 20 window constructs. Means were formed by averaging windows within parents, parents within viral genera and viral genera within strata. Five hundred resamples of whole viral genera within the corresponding host-genus support set retained all parent/window/treatment/background pairings. The same saved resampling draws were used for matching strata and paired contrasts. Intervals are pointwise 95% percentile intervals, without multiplicity adjustment. They are conditional on the selected viral genera and fixed chromosomes, and do not estimate uncertainty over a host-strain population. Parent-level resampling was retained as a sensitivity analysis. The 60 and 120 kb strata are feasibility-limited secondary analyses, with only one to three supported viral genera; a zero-width interval for a single genus does not demonstrate high precision.

The protocol set two engineering guideposts before C outcomes were available: mean viral-base retention of at least 95% and mean host-base removal of at least 50% in each primary stratum. These are use-case tolerances, not established biological standards, individual-sequence guarantees or simultaneous statistical confidence requirements. Failure under either endpoint is retained in the results.

## 8.3 Exploratory results and transport across length distributions

Under B's original equal-parent and equal-fragment-fraction weighting, predicted trimming removed 48.57% and 78.39% of host bases at 10% and 20% flanks while retaining 99.76% and 99.47% of viral bases, respectively (Table S35). Discarding flagged constructs lost 62.33% and 87.67% of viral bases. Filtered VFDB-positive full parents numbered only two of 30, with none positive under the strict thresholds. These results describe the selected reference panel and its three fixed backgrounds, not performance throughout the local environmental catalogue.

The local catalogue contains 3,060 contigs, of which 62.39% are 10–20 kb long. After the B results, the C1 contract specified transport to this observed whole-contig length distribution using fixed bins of 10–<15, 15–<20, 20–<40, 40–<80 and at least 80 kb. Constructs below 10 kb were excluded from the target-weighted summaries. Windows were averaged within parent and length bin, then across parents, before applying the local bin frequencies. Parent and construct support are retained by bin, host genus, flank proportion and treatment (Tables S36–S38). An unsupported bin invalidates the full target-weighted estimand; its weight was not redistributed to supported bins. Five hundred parent-genome resamples quantified uncertainty, and a full interval was withheld whenever resamples lacked complete bin support. This analysis is retrospective relative to B but follows the prespecified C1 transport protocol.

Predicted host-base removal after transport was 20.00% (95% interval 15.81%–24.49%) at 10% flanks and 46.85% (39.71%–54.26%) at 20% flanks; viral-base retention was 99.89% and 99.59%, respectively. The changed weighting defines a different summary, not a paired decline in method performance. For the displayed 20%-flank, whole-discard estimate, only 499 of 500 resamples supported all bins, so no full 95% interval is reported (Supplementary Figure S3). Missing intervals are not zero-width intervals. Transport by observed whole-contig length does not control other differences in composition, lineage or background, and the resulting estimates are not measured environmental trimming accuracy. This length variable also differs from C's known viral-window length before flanks are added.

Construction geometry dominates the transported values. Flanks were defined as a fraction of total construct length, so reweighting toward short local contigs also reweights toward very short flanks. The 10–15 kb bin carries 44.2% of the target weight; in that bin a 10% flank has a median of 565 bp on each side of the viral window, CheckV flagged 3 of 28 such constructs, and the construct-level mean host removal was 5.3%. The transported estimates therefore describe this construction convention applied to short windows. They are not the trimming accuracy expected for a local 10 kb contig carrying a host segment of unknown length.

## 8.4 Panel C: high average retention does not ensure complete host removal

Across the 36 primary predicted-trimming strata, mean viral-base retention ranged from 97.0% to 100.0%, and all mean estimates exceeded the 95% guidepost. Two corresponding interval lower bounds were below 95%. Mean host-base removal was below 50% in 24 of 36 strata, so the paired engineering goals were not met throughout the primary panel (Table S39 and Supplementary Figure S4). At the individual-construct level, 33 of 720 primary flanked constructs retained less than 95% of their viral sequence, with a minimum of 64.02% (Table S47). Average retention is consequently not a guarantee for a particular sequence.

Low mean host removal is mainly a detection outcome; incomplete removal after detection contributes less. Under predicted trimming a construct without a provirus flag is retained whole, so its host removal is exactly zero; this held for all 315 unflagged primary flanked constructs. Pooled across constructs rather than averaged within parents and viral genera, the 405 flagged constructs lost 71.2% of their host bases on average (median 50.0%, range 14.8%–100%). Flag rates rose with both viral window length and flank proportion:

| Viral window | Flagged at 10% flanks | Flagged at 20% flanks |
|---|---:|---:|
| 12.5 kb | 17 of 120 (14.2%) | 68 of 120 (56.7%) |
| 17.5 kb | 39 of 120 (32.5%) | 93 of 120 (77.5%) |
| 30 kb | 77 of 120 (64.2%) | 111 of 120 (92.5%) |

Across all 720 primary flanked constructs, 405 were flagged. Panel B shows the same gradient over fragment fractions, from 14 of 60 constructs at 25% of the parent with 10% flanks to 29 of 30 full parents with 20% flanks, and 395 of its 540 flanked constructs were flagged. No construct without an added flank was flagged in either panel: 0 of 270 in B and 0 of 242 in C, the latter including the 30 full parents. These are repeated constructs from 30 parents per panel, not independent samples. Counts come from the saved CheckV outputs through `dev/370-audit-integration-2026-09-26/calibration_detection.py` (outputs `detection_by_stratum.tsv`, `host_removal_by_detection.tsv` and `zero_flank_flags.tsv`).

Positive viral-retention differences and negative host-removal differences are constrained by the treatment definitions, so their magnitude, rather than their sign alone, is the calibration result. The zero line marks equal endpoints, not equivalence. The original and alternative chromosome backgrounds remain fixed. Source: Table S40.](figures/SF5_treatment_tradeoff.png){#sfig-sf5 width=100%}

The 18 primary background comparisons paired the same parent, viral window and flank proportion under the two corresponding bacterial chromosomes (Table S41 and Supplementary Figure S6). New-minus-original differences ranged from −1.08 to +2.47 percentage points for viral retention and −10.23 to +29.97 for host removal. They have no uniform direction. The background contrasts combine strain-sequence differences with different sampled chromosomal insertion locations; they are not isolated strain effects. Parent-level rather than viral-genus resampling changed whether three primary host-removal background intervals included zero, reinforcing the limited support for detailed between-background claims.

![Paired fixed-background differences under predicted trimming in panel C (Supplementary Figure S6). Differences are the alternative chromosome/position combination minus the original one, in percentage points, across 18 primary host-genus, window-length and flank-proportion strata. Each point uses five viral genera, ten parents and 20 matched viral windows per background; bars are pointwise 95% intervals from 500 viral-genus resamples preserving pairing. Backgrounds differ in both bacterial strain sequence and sampled insertion location. The zero line marks no difference, and intervals that include it do not establish equivalence. Intervals are unadjusted for multiple comparisons and do not estimate population-level host-strain variation. Source: Table S41.](figures/SF6_background_differences.png){#sfig-sf6 width=100%}

## 8.5 Baseline ORF retention, exact recall and VFDB target recovery

The 30 full, unflanked C parents yielded 3,011 baseline ORFs. This is a computational gene-calling baseline, not an experimentally verified gene set. For each construct, let $A$ be the baseline ORFs wholly contained in its input viral window; boundary-truncated baseline genes are ineligible. Let $K$ be those whose complete sequence remains within one retained interval, and $E$ those re-called at exactly the same coordinates and strand with an identical predicted protein sequence. The common-denominator fractions $(A-K)/A$, $(K-E)/A$ and $E/A$ respectively describe incomplete sequence retention, retained sequence without exact recall, and exact recall, and sum to one when $A>0$. The conditional fraction $E/K$ answers a different question and is undefined at $K=0$ (Tables S42 and S49). Discarded inputs remain in the total-loss endpoint rather than disappearing from the analysis.

Across 720 primary flanked constructs, the pooled eligible count was 18,408 baseline ORF occurrences; these repeat parent genes across windows, flank proportions and backgrounds (Table S50). Predicted trimming retained 18,314 occurrences and exactly recovered 17,674. Known-boundary trimming retained all 18,408 but exactly recovered only 17,804, leaving 604 retained occurrences without an exact recall. Thus even correct sequence boundaries can change gene calls relative to the full parent, and an exact-call difference is not itself evidence of biological gene or function loss. Whole-discard retained 6,814 occurrences and exactly recovered 6,564: its conditional recall was 96.33%, but its recovery relative to all eligible baseline occurrences was only 35.66%. Across the full panel, 516 whole-discard rows had no retained eligible ORF and an undefined conditional recall.

After the prespecified window-to-parent-to-viral-genus averaging, mean complete baseline-sequence retention under predicted trimming ranged from 98.28% to 100.00% across primary strata; exact recall ranged from 87.85% to 99.32%. These ranges come from different strata and are not additive. Supplementary Figure S7 shows the three components with their shared eligible-ORF denominator. The intervals quantify consistency of computational baseline recovery, not functional sensitivity.

![Decomposition of baseline ORF recovery after predicted trimming in panel C (Supplementary Figure S7). The denominator is the set of full-parent ORFs wholly contained in the input viral window. The rows show the fraction not retained completely, the fraction retained without exact recall, and the fraction recalled at identical coordinates and strand with an identical predicted protein sequence. Each primary stratum contains five viral genera, ten parents and 20 constructs; points average window-level fractions within parents and viral genera, and bars are pointwise 95% intervals from 500 viral-genus resamples. The three mean fractions sum to 100% within a stratum, but their interval bounds must not be added. Rows use different vertical scales. These are gene-calling consistency endpoints, not biological function measurements. Sources: Tables S42 and S49; pooled repeated-occurrence counts are reported separately in Table S50.](figures/SF7_orf_recovery.png){#sfig-sf7 width=100%}

Only six of 30 C parents, spanning three viral genera, carried filtered baseline VFDB hits (22 ORFs); four parents in two viral genera carried strict hits (12 ORFs; Table S43). Both are below the protocol's ten-positive-parent rule, so homology recovery remains descriptive without a stable functional-sensitivity claim. Ten positive parents is a pilot reporting rule, not a universal precision guarantee, and repeated windows cannot increase the independent positive support.

For VFDB recovery, $A$ and $K$ count eligible baseline-hit occurrences and their complete sequence retention. The exact-coordinate/same-target endpoint requires a re-called ORF at the original coordinates and strand to match the same best passing VFDB target; unlike the ORF endpoint above, it does not additionally require protein-sequence identity. For the primary filtered layer, predicted trimming gave $A=164$, $K=157$ and 155 exact-coordinate/same-target recoveries; the strict layer gave 92, 88 and 86. These are repeated occurrences, not independent positive genes. Target-set recovery alone can occur at a different gene coordinate and is not the same-gene endpoint. Strata without eligible baseline hits retain undefined ratios rather than 0% or 100% recovery (Tables S44 and S50). No VFDB recovery measure here establishes virulence activity or transmission potential.

## 8.6 Reference proximity and the boundary of generalization

All 30 full C parents had a reported CheckV reference average amino-acid identity (AAI) of at least 95%, with a minimum of 95.09%; 18 were reported at 100% (Table S45). The whole panel, full-parent baseline and unflanked-window cohorts overlap and cannot be summed as independent samples (Table S46). Five unflanked windows had AAI below 95%, but their three full parents all remained at least 95%, so those windows do not form an independent distant-reference parent group. Reported 100% AAI is not a claim of whole-genome nucleotide identity, and the CheckV completeness-confidence category is not a confidence assessment of this calibration's boundary accuracy [@nayfach2021checkv].

Panel C therefore expands viral genera relative to B while remaining close to the CheckV reference database. Neither panel establishes performance for distant-reference environmental viruses, validates the biological origin of all local VFDB hits, or supplies independent replication for the 38 global anti-defense-profile slopes. The B and C constructs are not pooled as 1,900 independent samples. Their roles are controlled calibration, length-distribution sensitivity and explicit documentation of what sequence retention and annotation recovery can and cannot support.

# Supplementary Note 9. Agreement between saved local annotations

Across the same 3,060-vOTU catalogue, dbAPIS and DefenseFinder antidefense annotations shared 99 carrier vOTUs, with 616 and seven carriers unique to their respective outputs and 2,338 negative in both (Cohen’s κ = 0.192445; Jaccard index = 0.137119). PADLOC and DefenseFinder defense calls shared one carrier, with 30 and four unique carriers and 3,025 negative in both (κ = 0.052890; Jaccard = 0.028571). Thus, the 31-to-five count contrast does not represent nested retention under successively stricter criteria ([Table S51](tables/S51_cross_library.tsv), [Table S52](tables/S52_carrier_membership.tsv)).

The antidefense outputs shared 110 exact ORF identifiers. This is separate from the vOTU-level κ and does not define a common ORF testing universe. A verified common universe of scanned ORFs was not available for this comparison, so an ORF-level κ was not estimated. Seven candidate target-label mappings are supplied as inventory comparisons, without treating their models or thresholds as equivalent ([Table S53](tables/S53_target_overlap.tsv)). These results describe agreement among saved outputs, not sensitivity or accuracy against functional truth. Marginal prevalence and library scope affect agreement statistics.

Methods: complete binary carriage tables were constructed over all catalogue vOTUs. Cohen’s κ was computed as (observed agreement − marginal-expected agreement)/(1 − marginal-expected agreement); Jaccard overlap used the union of positive carriers as its denominator. Exact ORF identifiers were intersected separately. The saved SQLite database was accessed read-only, and input SHA256 fingerprints were unchanged across the audit.

# Supplementary Note 10. Archived profile-level negative-background control

Among 356 profiles, 12 produced at least one hit to reversed or doublet-shuffled proteins; all 12 were in the GA ≤25 stratum. These archived controls belong to the separate defense-census resource. Each decoy design contained 4,984,480 proteins, and the real database contained 369,281,941 proteins. For each profile, rates were calculated per million proteins with their respective denominators. The larger decoy rate was divided by the real-database rate. Five profiles met the archived operational review trigger of a ratio ≥0.10: Dpd__DpdI, gnarl1, acrie6, acriia26 and acriia30. Ten profiles had no real-database hits, so their ratios were undefined; they were not counted as passing ([Table S54](tables/S54_decoy_profiles.tsv), [Table S55](tables/S55_decoy_strata.tsv), [Table S56](tables/S56_decoy_flags.tsv)).

| GA stratum | Profiles | Any decoy hit | Reversed profile–protein pairs | Doublet profile–protein pairs | Zero real hits | Review flags |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| ≤25 | 107 | 12 | 17 | 5 | 0 | 5 |
| (25,100] | 135 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2 | 0 |
| >100 | 114 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 8 | 0 |

The counts are distinct protein hits within each profile at the archived scanning criteria and a profile-coverage threshold of 0.35. Cross-profile sums are profile–protein pairs, not globally deduplicated proteins. We recomputed archived count summaries without rerunning the HMM searches. The ratio is an operational investigation measure, not an estimated biological false-discovery rate. This control does not provide system-level validation or demonstrate biological function. The absence of observed decoy hits does not establish zero error. The 38 primary profiles all occur by name in this table; only ulx has nonzero decoy hits and none meets the trigger. Name matching does not establish identical HMM bytes or scanning conditions.

# Supplementary Note 11. Proportional composition sensitivity

This analysis estimates domain-instance proportions, rather than the feature-carriage log-odds slopes in Note 5. The domain-instance proportion analysis used 66,089 genomes with at least ten annotated Pfam instances. The frozen classification included 285 METAB, 149 REPL, 183 STRUCT, 77 REG and 1,134 OTHER domains. Repeated domain occurrences were retained; 25,291 unbinned instances remained in the denominator of 1,488,788 instances. For each of the six components, including zero-count genomes, we fitted a weighted linear regression of its fraction against log10(CDS count), using annotated-instance count as the genome weight. Full-cohort intervals use a CR1 sandwich estimator clustered by gene-sharing group, with finite-sample factor G/(G−1) × (n−1)/(n−2) and a t reference with G−1 degrees of freedom; G = 25,494. Genome-level HC3 intervals are also supplied ([Table S57](tables/S57_full_proportions.tsv)).

We reused 50 frozen selections, each containing one genome per gene-sharing group from the 77,951-genome source cohort, before applying the ten-instance filter. Excluded representatives were not replaced. Each selection retained 24,882–24,939 genomes. All 300 category fits were estimable, and independent R and Python slope calculations differed by at most 4.35 × 10⁻¹⁵ ([Table S58](tables/S58_proportion_replicates.tsv), [Table S59](tables/S59_proportion_summary.tsv), [Table S60](tables/S60_selection_accounting.tsv)). These remain instance-weighted analyses; one selected genome per group does not make the groups equally weighted.

| Category | Full-cohort slope, percentage points per ten-fold CDS increase | CR1 95% interval | Median over 50 selections | 2.5th–97.5th selection percentiles |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| METAB | 16.329 | 15.087 to 17.570 | 15.830 | 15.710 to 15.961 |
| REPL | 5.647 | 4.318 to 6.976 | 4.608 | 4.510 to 4.701 |
| STRUCT | −25.073 | −26.918 to −23.228 | −21.874 | −21.978 to −21.761 |
| REG | −0.752 | −1.257 to −0.246 | −0.850 | −0.890 to −0.799 |
| OTHER | 0.363 | −1.363 to 2.089 | −1.623 | −1.754 to −1.417 |
| unbinned_rare | 3.486 | 2.774 to 4.199 | 3.892 | 3.754 to 3.976 |

Selection percentiles describe variation across fixed representatives, conditional on the source cohort; they are not population confidence intervals (Supplementary Figure S8). METAB/REPL slopes were positive and STRUCT/REG slopes negative in all 50 selections. Three boundaries apply. First, the full-cohort OTHER interval spans zero (−1.363 to 2.089), whereas the OTHER slope was negative in all 50 selections, so neither the sign nor the size of this residual component is resolved; it is retained in full. Second, for STRUCT the selection range (−21.978 to −21.761) lies entirely outside the full-cohort CR1 interval (−26.918 to −23.228), and the OTHER selection range likewise lies below its full-cohort interval: representative selection changes the estimated magnitude, not only its precision. Third, these slopes describe annotated-domain composition; they do not demonstrate metabolic activity, expression or fitness effects. The six fractions sum to one, so their slopes are coupled; these six components are not independent replications of a class contrast. Annotation coverage, multidomain proteins and keyword classification affect the interpretation. For example, the frozen mapping assigns pfam03641, a putative lysine-decarboxylase domain, to STRUCT through the substring “lysin” ([Table S61](tables/S61_domain_mapping.tsv)). No post hoc category correction was applied. The results do not establish phylogenetic independence or a causal allocation mechanism.

![Annotated-domain composition sensitivity (Supplementary Figure S8). (A) Full-cohort WLS slopes and CR1 95% confidence intervals clustered by gene-sharing group. (B) Median slopes over 50 fixed representative selections and their 2.5th–97.5th percentiles, which are not population confidence intervals. Both panels retain domain-count weights and all denominator components. Values are percentage-point changes per ten-fold increase in CDS count. Source data in Table S64 are fractions per log10 unit; multiply by 100 for the displayed units. ](figures/SF8_proportional_sensitivity.png){#sfig-sf8 width=100%}

Historical replication limitation: these frozen representatives did not exactly reproduce the separate archived j40 K4 feature-carriage log-odds contrast. The observed median and percentiles were 2.77913 [2.59099, 2.93695], versus archived 2.7747 [2.602, 2.919]. The historical ordered sampling frame and selection membership were unavailable in the inspected archive. Its cause remains unresolved. The proportional result is therefore a separate sensitivity, not an exact replication of the historical sampling. The original K4 failure record is preserved in the accompanying code and evidence package.

# Supplementary Note 12. Recovered historical run versions

The VIBRANT 1.2.1 run log dated 2 May 2026 accompanies 784 AMG rows that reproduce the complete SQLite AMG row multiset. Quality/type records match all 3,060 catalogue rows, including four with no VIBRANT source record. The six geNomad modules of the 1 May 2026 clust_votu.fasta run each record version 1.11.1; their JSON input MD5s match the archived FASTA, and the saved summary matches catalogue score/topology values for all 3,060 vOTUs. The annotate and find-proviruses logs identify database v1.9. Its complete database hash manifest remains unavailable.

The local dbAPIS hmmscan report records HMMER 3.4. All 950 retained query/profile/E-value/score tuples occur in that report; applying the documented import filter to the source annotation table reproduces all 950 SQLite rows. E-values were normalized to 12 significant digits to reconcile binary floating-point roundtrips. This version applies to the local dbAPIS run; the HMMER version used by the global companion antidefense arm remains unverified ([Table S62](tables/S62_run_versions.tsv), [Table S63](tables/S63_version_checks.tsv)). Original small logs and module metadata are retained in the accompanying historical-run evidence; the large HMMER report is represented by a verbatim header excerpt and full-file SHA256, not a full copy.
